A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Dropsembles work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy-classification, MNIST reconstruction, corrupted-atlas, and lumbar MRI experiments, including numerical comparisons and qualitative reconstructions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ShapeNet experiments, lumbar ensemble comparisons, and additional sensitivity analyses.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains dropout pretraining, sampling fixed thinned networks, independent fine-tuning, and prediction aggregation. The EWC objective is unchanged. DeepSDF and SIREN are new experimental configurations of the existing general framework, rather than revisions to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds ShapeNet airplane reconstruction using signed distance functions and eroded inputs, extending evaluation to non-anatomical 3D shapes and an additional implicit representation. The toy, MNIST, corrupted-atlas, and MRI coverage remains.

E2.justification: v1 explicitly omitted full deep ensembles from lumbar experiments because of computational cost. v2 evaluates them on corrupted-atlas and MRI reconstruction in Tables 2, 6, and 7, substantially strengthening the central comparison. MC dropout + EWC rows disappear from those comparisons, although that method remains elsewhere. Toy and MNIST comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: MNIST evaluation expands from three to 20 test images. ShapeNet introduces 1,000 training shapes, ten unseen corrupted shapes, SDF training/fine-tuning protocols, SIREN configurations, and mIoU reporting. Figure 9 additionally varies the number of thinned networks. The new general statement that all models use four instances conflicts with Appendix C's retained 100 MC-dropout samples for the toy task.

E4.justification: The original EWC-strength sweeps are retained as Figures 6–8. v2 adds network-count sensitivity experiments for toy classification and MNIST in Figure 9, SIREN configuration comparisons, a lumbar thin-structure case study in Figure 5, and a ShapeNet smoothness comparison in Figure 11.

E5.justification: Both versions report three random seeds for toy results and use numerical dispersion and shaded uncertainty bands. v2 establishes no new repeated-run count, significance test, or uncertainty-estimation procedure. The MNIST increase concerns distinct test images, not repeated seeds; additional result rows and plots continue the existing reporting style.

E6.justification: v2 adds ShapeNet, SIREN, lumbar ensemble, sensitivity, and training-time results. Table 1 replaces three-image MNIST results with 20-image results; for example, MC-dropout DSC changes from 58.2% to 54.8%, which is not a same-setting deterioration. Lumbar MC-dropout HD changes from 13.1 to 18.15 in Table 2 despite unchanged per-case values in the appendix. Some MRI entries also change; toy results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, dataset assumptions, prediction mixture, and EWC formulation are retained. Appendix A preserves the same Bayes/Laplace/Fisher derivation and Equations 3–5. Notational clarification does not introduce new mathematical reasoning or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 narrows the novelty framing to epistemic uncertainty in the implicit decoder during fine-tuning and adds an explicit first-of-its-kind contribution for fine-tuning from synthetic data. The central claims of ensemble-like accuracy/calibration with lower computational cost and EWC-assisted adaptation remain.

C2.justification: The lumbar EWC discussion changes from insignificant benefits attributed to difficult regularization selection to preservation of thin structures that Dice overlooks and Hausdorff distance better captures. v2 removes the warning that four network samples introduce moderate variability, while retaining the limitation of ensemble-like fine-tuning costs.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds substantial ShapeNet/SIREN reproduction details: occupancy resolution, SDF construction, clipped versus unclipped L1 losses, learning rates, epoch budgets, and dropout placement. It newly documents MNIST encoder pooling without establishing an architecture change. Tables 2 and 5 add stage-specific lumbar training costs, although some Table 5 totals are arithmetically inconsistent. The code-access link remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Shen et al. (2021), Yang et al. (2023), and representation literature supporting the SIREN experiments. It more explicitly distinguishes decoder epistemic uncertainty from encoder and aleatoric uncertainty modeling. Most related work remains; the switch to author–date citations is stylistic.

P1.justification: The introduction's uncertainty framing and portions of the experimental discussion and conclusion are rewritten, with smaller terminology, affiliation, and acknowledgment edits. The overall section sequence and most existing methodological exposition remain, so this is a limited narrative revision.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 5 and 9–13 and Tables 3–5, expands Table 1 with ShapeNet columns, and replaces Table 2's inference-time column with training/fine-tuning times. Existing figures and regularization plots are largely retained and repositioned within the conference layout. Figure 9 incorrectly carries a lumbar-reconstruction caption despite displaying network-count sensitivity plots.

improvement.justification: v1 omitted deep ensembles from its demanding lumbar application, leaving an important gap in evidence for the central quality-versus-cost claim. v2 supplies that comparison: Table 2 reports DSC of 86.8% for Dropsembles versus 86.5% for ensembles, with pretraining costs of 48 versus 192 GPU-hours. ShapeNet/SIREN tests and the larger MNIST evaluation further strengthen empirical support. The incorrect Figure 9 caption, timing arithmetic errors, and inconsistent MC-dropout summary values reduce reporting reliability, but do not outweigh the substantial gain from directly testing the central comparison.
